items.gist: The heart is the tattva, and prāṇa is described through laya and udaya, including sixty-year reckoning and activity variety.
Kālaśakti lies outside; its form is not fixed, and it appears variously in dream, sleep, and samādhi.
Apāna spreads from the heart through the mūla-pīṭha, while Brahmā and others are worshipped by yogis as pervading the universe.
Brahmā and others preside over bodies and rebirth, but in mukti the supreme Devī remains; knowing this grants dīkṣā.
Śiva as causeless cause is known, and worship destroys the dualistic adhovaktra; sixty-year reckoning applies at apāna's rise.
Tuṭi and related measures are distributed through the nāḍīs, which spread in ten directions and pervade the body.

items.topic: Three main nāḍīs and prāṇa counts
items.gist: Prāṇa moves through the three principal nāḍīs of moon, sun, and fire, carrying nine hundred prāṇas over day and night.
The text details viṣuvat days, saṃkrānti transitions, and prāṇa counts through day and night.
Night and day are analyzed through increase, decrease, saṃkrānti, and viṣuvat, with balanced movement.
Samāna time is reckoned subtly, including sandhyā and other divisions, with internal saṃkrānti as primary.
Udāna is treated like prāṇa's pervasion, while vyāna is all-pervading and free from sequence.
Creation, dissolution, stability, and grace are assigned to times, and one nāda-varṇa is identified with Bhairava and Parā Devī.
Short vowels and entry syllables are mapped to bodily locations such as dvādaśānta, forehead, throat, and heart.
The varṇa continuum arises within locations, prāṇa is the heart's form, and parodaya is described as subtle.
Mātrās and half-mātrās are enumerated, leading to the eighty-one-pada mantra and Devī.
Śiva is known through parāmarśa, and the pada is completed as the eighty-one-pada reflection is fulfilled.
The gross method uses mātrās, half-mātrās, aṅgula divisions, and long and pluta measures.
Kṣakāra is the universal gatherer of all conjunctions and arises at all varṇa junctions.
The thirty-six course of varṇas yields cruel and gentle results, and hṛdyakāra with hakāra is aham advaita.
The eighty-one mātrās circulate through the aṅgulas, and the subtle udaya is threefold while gross udaya is now described.
